Nvidia dispelled fears of the AI trade slowing with one simple number: FY28 revenue growth is guided to be 75%, up from 70%, despite a higher FY27 base. Rubin’s first quarter is nearly double Blackwell’s at $20B vs $11B.

THE CARNAGE IS REAL

It’s so fascinating looking at how wrecked some of these sectors are. With all the attention on semis, it’s easy to not notice that quantums, nuclear, clean energy, optical names, and more have fully retraced all the euphoria of the last year.

Type these up: $OKLO $QUBT $QBTS $ASTS $FLNC $EOSE $AAOI $AXTI

Nuclear was promises of “a new paradigm”. Quantum was the same.

This supercycle in semis is nothing like that in that these are real businesses w real valuations, but it is valid to ask this: 

Should the whole upmove and euphoria of the last year never have occurred? Probably so.

That said, the level of panic now is approaching the euphoria we saw then.

Unlike with quantum and the bs names, I do suspect some sharp analyst that understands the semis/cloud and isn’t high on hopium is going to find some real gems once the dust settles.

And as for traders… the right equilibrium is going to be somewhere in between. But capturing that means waiting for the backside, utilizing the right side of the V, and following proper risk management.

We tested this. Every SPY session since 2003 with volume under half its 50-day average: 138 days.

SPY was higher 10 days later 71.7% of the time. Any day: 62.2%. Statistically significant (p = 0.022).

After our April post, four days triggered it. All four were higher 20 days later: +8.97%, +8.56%, +4.95%, +4.21%.

This doesn't mean low volume causes rallies. It means low volume isn't a warning sign. The data says "don't dismiss it," not "volume doesn't matter.”

Low volume isn't a warning sign. It's an auction, and quiet auctions still clear higher.

posts.name: Brian Shannon, CMT ⚓️
posts.text:
Volume by price charts show where the crowd has the strongest "memory." 

More people are anchored to those levels as important because that's where the most shares changed hands.

They're another way, like the 200 SMA, the YTD VWAP  or the 🟢VWAP from the 2025 tariff low, to find LEVELS of INTEREST.

We don't treat downside levels of interest as support to stick a bid in. They're places where there may be enough demand to offset supply and absorb it without further price deterioration.

That process usually starts with short covering, slowly at first. Then come bargain hunters who are guessing. Finally, large institutions slow their selling, and smarter institutions with plenty of cash start building positions.

Wait for evidence the flames have died down and the embers have cooled before you jump into the fire pit.

posts.name: Daniel Koss
posts.text:
Since all the questions are the same, I'll answer them here:

1) When is the bottom in? 

Obviously nobody knows. When everyone on margin is liquidated, maybe 🌝

2) Are you selling everything? 

Of course not. It's time to massively buy here. The time to sell was if you saw it coming or while it happened and if you understood early what the magnitude would be. Prices now are getting so low that in the long term returns will be crazy good. Doesn't mean we can't go much lower in the short term. But selling here is way to risky for me.

3) How did you trade this?

I didn't. I completely missed this one and am bagholding bad over the last 2 months like almost everyone else. I got complacent. Will talk about the mistakes I made and what I learned from it in the Substack post later today.

4) Are we cooked?

No. If you got margin called or did other gambles like short dated options, 3x ETFs etc - yeah your money is gone. If you're just holding long and strong we're completely fine. This deleveraging and liquidity issue doesn't break the thesis for AI hyperbulls at all! The gains over multiple years will still be generational.

5) When will we reach new ATH?

"Years?! WTF when are we up again?"

Obviously I have no clue when liquidity could improve. I don't know when the Iran war will end or what the FED will do. This crash felt entirely preventable and to some degree intentionally made. I think it could easily take until H2 2027 to reach new ATH. Not the timeline we all wanted, but better get comfortable that we now might be bagholding for quite a while. We need liquidity and macro will dictate our timeline.

In general my advice to stay sane is to simply look at a longer 3-5 year time horizon. Do you really think ANY macro can prevent stocks from ripping up again over that time horizon? The real winners will not stay this cheap for that long.

So the only people I think will stay bagholders are the ones who got liquidated or keep holding the shitcos that go bankrupt or won't recover because their earnings will keep disappointing.

quoted.text:
Here's why everything is crashing 📉

(this is my guess, but I believe the data strongly supports it)

1) AI is the biggest technological innovation ever.
2) Everyone has started to agree over the last 3 years.
3) Because everyone knows this is happening, many investors express this view with mind-blowing amounts of leverage, to the degree that it doesn't matter at all if they are right or wrong, because a tiny correction will liquidate them.
4) Leverage in the AI trade ($NVDA $MU $SOXL $TQQQ) has reached historic record levels.
(Data: US margin debt hit an all-time record of $1.50T in June 2026 and was still $1.45T at the end of October, per FINRA's latest monthly data.)
5) Inevitably, something bad happens (Iran, inflation, rate hikes, Dems winning the midterms, data center delays at $CRWV $NBIS $ORCL, Jensen leaving $NVDA, pick your poison).
6) A tiny, even if absolutely deserved, correction gets massively amplified beyond anything that makes sense, because every drop leads to liquidations, stop losses, and some people ape back in and double down on margin. FORCED selling leads to forced selling leads to forced selling.

On Anthropic’s first day of trading, the way they handled things was truly disgraceful.

The initial offering price was originally set at $70–$78, but it was raised straight to $83. Not only did they raise the price, but they also increased the number of shares offered from the planned 820 million to 980 million—a jump of nearly 20%.

At least with instant noodles, they usually offer more for the same price—but Anthropic went and did both: increasing the quantity and the price.

Even more outrageous is that on the very first day of trading, management cashed out $2 billion.

Are they really that desperate? They could at least put on a show—don’t rush to cash out right after going public. How are retail investors supposed not to be scared by that?

And that’s not all.

Reportedly, 10% of employee stock options were unlocked on the first day of trading—amounting to approximately 300 million shares, equivalent to nearly one-third of the total offering.

What’s truly hair-raising is the unlocking schedule that follows.

A batch will be unlocked in mid-December, followed by successive unlockings in early, mid, and late January 2027. Throughout the first quarter of 2027, the total volume of shares expected to be unlocked is projected to reach 3 billion.

What does that mean?

The total offering size is only 980 million shares, yet the number of shares set to be unlocked in just one quarter is more than three times that amount.

This isn’t a gradual release of shares—it’s a barrage

$KOS $GLNG I wonder whether weakness in Komos and Golar is related to the news that BP is looking to divest its majority stake and operatorship of the GTA liquefied natural gas facility off the coast of West Africa. If so, the market’s ignorance could be giving us an amazing opportunity, since it would be a huge catalyst for both stocks. But I’m not sure that’s the case; I suspect recession fears are behind the sell-off in many other energy names, even though oil prices have held up quite well.

Meg O'Neill became CEO of BP in April 2026. She's taking on a tough job with a weak team and a heavy workload. She needs quick wins—or she may not be in the role in two years—so M&A could provide one. It was well known that she put the UK, Egypt, and GTA up for sale, and I expect GTA to be sold by 2027. 

BP has been a pain in the ass for Kosmos, Mauritania and Senegal: the GTA partnership. First, the cost overruns and delays are attributed solely to BP, leaving Mauritania and Senegal furious and prompting them to launch an audit of the project costs. Following the audit, Senegalese Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko criticised the GTA contract as "one-sided and unfair" in a March 2026 televised address, as Senegal weighed legal options and contract renegotiations. Moreover, back in 2020, BP signed the marketing agreement at a very profitable rate, while the economics of the GTA partnership are less attractive, at least until 2033, when the gas contract ends and the GTA group can choose to extend it or find another offtaker on better terms. The reality is that BP built the foundations, but its inability to increase production—due to poor relations with the government and a loss of focus—is undermining the project’s economics. For example, Golar has an incentive to replace Gimi (2.4 MPTA) with a potential MK3 (5 MPTA), a move that would significantly improve ROI because the GTA partnership requires minimal investment (FPSO debottlenecking and some additional wells). However, BP has not supported the idea, as its focus has been elsewhere.

In summary, BP is a forced seller because of its poor historical management of the project. This is a very interesting asset for Middle Eastern players looking to diversify their gas production, especially after the Hormuz problems. It has high-quality gas, is very close to Europe, and offers huge reserves and development potential. The sale will bring short-term benefits to Kosmos, such as lower operating expenses, since BP personnel are the largest cost. In the medium term, it could benefit both Kosmos and Golar by refocusing on Phase 2 and potentially bringing a Golar vessel back into the equation.

THE MAST DISCLOSURE: WHAT THE BIS LICENSE RECORDS ACTUALLY SHOW

On November 19, 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, chaired by Rep. Brian Mast, publicly released Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) export license application information for NVIDIA and AMD AI chip sales to China. The release is stronger and weaker than the headline at the same time: stronger, because the government's own license table puts the Megaspeed channel's entities inside NVIDIA's applications, including one direct application to a Megaspeed-network company; weaker, because the same table shows zero shipments against the approvals as of May 11, 2026, the two largest asks returned without action, and only previous-generation chips throughout.

WHAT WAS RELEASED, AND UNDER WHAT AUTHORITY

• The legal vehicle is the Export Control Reform Act disclosure provision, 50 U.S.C. 4820(h)(2)(B)(ii): the committee determined that withholding the information is contrary to the national interest. The underlying BIS table is marked CUI//SP-EXPT, statutorily protected export information, releasable only on that determination.
• Ranking Member Gregory Meeks supported the release and the committee approved the disclosure by unanimous consent, per the committee Democratic minority's account of the business meeting. The disclosure is bipartisan in form even though the framing language is the Republican chairman's.
• The committee called it the most detailed public disclosure in the history of the Export Control Reform Act.

THE NUMBERS, FROM THE DOCUMENTS THEMSELVES

The release has two documents: a committee summary and the BIS table "H200 License and Equivalent Application Status as of May 11, 2026." Every figure in this section is from those two documents.

• Covered products are only two: NVIDIA's H200 and AMD's MI325X. No Blackwell or newer parts appear anywhere in the record.
• Applications received by BIS as of May 11, 2026: 3,444,160 covered chips requested for PRC companies.
• Approved: 879,868 chips across 21 license applications, every one of them marked "Approved, not shipped," ultimate location China in all 21 cases: NVIDIA 579,868 across 17 applications, AMD 300,000 across 4 applications.
• Approvals to companies on the Department of War's 1260H Chinese Military Companies list total 272,000, 30.9 percent of approvals: Tencent and subsidiaries 150,000 (NVIDIA 75,000 to Tencent Technology (Shenzhen), application dated 12/19/2025; AMD 75,000 to Oriental Power Holdings, a Tencent subsidiary), Alibaba 75,000 (NVIDIA, application dated 12/16/2025), Baidu 43,000 (NVIDIA, 3/10/2026), BYD 4,000 (NVIDIA, 3/16/2026).
• Other approved consignees include ByteDance on both sides of the vendor split (NVIDIA 75,000 to Beijing Bytedance Technology; AMD 75,000 to Beijing Zitiao Network Technology, a ByteDance subsidiary), JD (41,300), DiDi (NVIDIA 24,780 plus AMD 75,000), Kuaishou (AMD 75,000), VNET (75,000), Linkwise Digital (75,000), Mihoyo (57,810), Ubiquant (8,660), Li Auto (8,260), Great Wall Motor (4,800), Shanghai Yovole (4,250), Tesla (Shanghai) (4,000), Shanghai Jiatang (4,000), and one 8-chip NVIDIA self-consigned application.
• Returned without action (RWA): 9 applications totaling 1,888,950 chips, including the two largest asks in the record: NVIDIA to Alibaba Group, 610,000 (2/6/2026), and NVIDIA to Bytedance System SDN BHD (Malaysia), 508,000 (12/11/2025). The remaining RWAs are offshore cloud asks (Alibaba Cloud Malaysia 50,500 and 203,000; PT Byteplus Indonesia 203,000; TikTok Thailand 154,000), an Alibaba 10,450, and AMD applications for http://JD.Com (75,000) and Huaxia (75,000). RWA is a return without action, not a formal denial; its practical effect is that the sale could not proceed on that application.

posts.name: Ben Woodward, CFA
posts.text:
In short: perma-anything is entertainment, not analysis. The market doesn't pay you for being consistently loud — it pays you for being occasionally right and properly sized.    

Why perma-bulls and perma-bears both fail:
• Perma-bulls (Tom Lee, Dan Ives) are right in the long run because markets trend up — but their calls are useless for timing. They're bullish in 2007, bullish in 2008, bullish in 2020. The broken clock eventually "works," but the drawdowns in between are brutal. And their optimism is often a business model: bullish calls generate TV appearances, client flow, and attention.
• Perma-bears (the perpetual doomers) have the opposite problem: they sound smart and rigorous, but being early is indistinguishable from being wrong. A bear who called 2008 in 2005 missed a 30%+ rally before being "vindicated." And perma-bears rarely flip bullish, so they miss every recovery. 
The uncomfortable middle: The people worth listening to are the ones who change their mind — who update on data rather than defend a brand. The problem is those voices are quieter, less entertaining, and don't fit the "personality" model that financial media rewards.
 
The real takeaway: Neither perma-bull nor perma-bear commentary is actionable on its own. What matters is the reasoning and the risk management — position sizing, stop losses, scenario planning. A perma-bull with a 2% position and a stop loss is more useful than a perma-bear with a 100% short and no exit plan.

quoted.text:
I’ve presented the $MRVL - for- $LITE merger proposal as a prime example of what can go wrong when a company uses its own stock to buy another company’s stock.  In just over a month, $MRVL’s stock has dropped by -45%, which has cut the +24% premium being paid for $LITE to a -41% discount vs $LITE’s stock price before the announcement. This occurs because of massive dilution to the acquiring company’s stock, plus arbitragers pre-selling shares of the acquirer rather than wait for the deal to close in 12-18 months.  

The same dynamic is likely when $SPCX offers a +24% premium for $TSLA using SPCX stock as currency:  TSLA investors will get a short-term pop on the deal headline and then experience quick downward pressure on $TSLA stock as investors sell $SPCX to try to lock in profits.

I would bet most $LITE investors would love to roll back the clock to Oct 28 when their stock was trading at $914 before MRVL’s offer to pay a +24% premium which on paper amounted to $1,132/share ($914 + 24%).  Instead $LITE stock is now DOWN -41% since the deal announcement to just $535/share today (-41% from $914 instead of a +24% premium).  If history repeats, TSLA at $374 today plus a +24% premium paid in SPCX shares (on paper worth $464/share) could be worth -25% less within a month ($280/share) given what could amount to 50% dilution to $SPCX, which could trade down by less than $MRVL since it’s not a pure AI play.

posts.name: Jose Najarro Stocks
posts.text:
SpaceX $SPCX just wrapped one of the biggest AI chip financings ever: about $32B of bonds backed by Nvidia Vera Rubin GPUs, per Bloomberg.

The biggest piece, a roughly $25.2B Class A-3 tranche, reportedly priced at an 8.259% yield. The market will say it is a hefty premium for investment grade paper when the average US high grade yield was 5.95% on Thursday.

The structure is the story. A bankruptcy remote trust called Saturn Funding Trust buys the Vera Rubin NVL72 equipment and leases it to SpaceX for about five years under a "hell-or-high-water" lease, so SpaceX keeps paying even if the GPUs fail, per KBRA's rating report. The debt stays off SpaceX's own balance sheet, and the full package reportedly tops $40B including bank loans.

One twist: lenders reportedly pushed for safeguards so the chips can't be launched into orbit, where they would be hard to repossess, per the FT. SpaceX says they're going into data centers on Earth.

My take: 8%+ on GPU collateral is the market telling you exactly how it prices AI hardware risk. Expect this template to get copied.

Caveat: the final size and yields come from Bloomberg, not a SpaceX release.

$NVDA $APO $GS $CRWV $TSLA

quoted.text:
Ok I do have a view on NVIDIA without Jensen. 
I’ll tell you the real reason $NVDA will likely fail without him and why the frontier labs and hyperscalers are the biggest winners. (Elon has been in a really good mood recently. Have you noticed?) 
The biggest threat to NVIDIA is its own customers, the frontier labs. NVIDIA has to become a frontier lab faster than frontier labs are becoming chip companies. And with Jensen out, they likely won't maintain the momentum to get there.
With recursive self-improvement (RSI), every frontier lab and hyperscaler must become a chip company or lose the AI race. It's that simple, and they've all laid the groundwork (Google TPUs, OpenAI and Meta building custom ASICs with Broadcom, Anthropic building an in-house silicon team, and SpaceX/xAI/Tesla building Terafab).
That's because software-only RSI has clear physical limits. Software can reduce how much computation and data movement a model needs, but it can't change the chip's physical bandwidth, memory capacity, or interconnect. Custom silicon gives labs another way to improve performance: designing the memory system, compute, and networking around their own workloads.
To get the real compounding effect of RSI, you have to co-design the model and the silicon so it becomes a two-way feedback loop: smarter models design better custom chips, and those chips train and run the next model faster. You can't do that on off-the-shelf NVIDIA GPUs because you get zero proprietary edge buying the same

posts.name: Rihard Jarc
posts.text:
Bought $ANT. What people fail to understand about $ANT is that, in recent months, the stakes of $ANT achieving a monopoly-like position have risen significantly.

$ANT has cracked distillation, so open-source models going forward will have a much harder time distilling their models and, with it, catching up in capability. The crackdown on chip exports to China is an additional blow to the Chinese open-source labs on top of Jensen not being at $NVDA anymore.

Even with US-based competition, $ANT, with their IPO, now has $250B in cash on the balance sheet and makes +$81B ARR. The real advantage here is that we are now entering the phase where training models has become really expensive, and with RSI, this will only accelerate, as the key thing when it comes to model training and the cadence of shipping in an RSI world will be the amount of compute that you have. As market conditions have worsened for both debt and equity, competitors like OpenAI will have a hard time securing funds (the latest round is already an example of that), which means the only two companies capable of chasing $ANT based on spend on compute may end up being $GOOGL and $META. With $META, even if they come to the frontier, their focus is on the consumer and won't be able to focus deeply on enterprise the way $ANT can.

When an AI lab has a frontier model and outside distillation can't happen, the inside distillation that $ANT can do is very valuable. If the gap on the frontier between $ANT and others widens (which I believe will be the case in the coming months), even their »cheap« models that were distilled from their best frontier model might be intelligence/cost wise better than the best models from their competitors, which gives $ANT the ability to capture the whole market.

As long as scaling laws hold and every new training run becomes a factor more expensive than the last one, AI models might not end up being a commodity, because the enormous cost of training is the barrier that forms the moat. The one who owns the best model, with a sufficient gap, also owns the cheapest model and can go deep in verticals and capture margin there, too. The chances for $ANT to achieve that have gone up substantially in the last few weeks.

I normally avoid IPOs, as they, in normal conditions, are not great timing-wise for buyers, as the sellers do them in great times for them. With $ANT, this is not the case in my view, as $ANT's management motivation is, at least in part, not driven by wealth and timing but more about securing their best long-term position, which, with this IPO, they did.

If sentiment for AI companies worsens, this actually helps $ANT in the long term, as they have done their job and can sleep soundly on capital for the next few years, while others will struggle.

I will write a more detailed analysis of $ANT and my decision in my newsletter in the coming days.

posts.text:
SpaceX’s, $SPCX, lenders want to stop it from launching $40 billion worth of AI chips into space, according to the Financial Times.

The chips back a roughly $40 billion financing deal led by Apollo. An Apollo-managed entity buys Nvidia GPUs and leases them to SpaceX, which pays it back over about five years. If SpaceX defaults, the lenders can take back the chips and sell them.

That’s the problem with space. Lenders worry that if SpaceX later sends the chips into orbit for its planned space-based data centers, they couldn’t reclaim them in a default. They’re now demanding legal protections to keep the chips on the ground.

SpaceX closed the deal in October, with the leases set to begin in the first half of 2027. Musk has said debt markets have “almost entirely shut off access to money” for AI companies without other big revenue streams.

posts.text:
If you're an $MSTR investor, grab a coffee and get comfortable.

Natalie Brunell's Q&A with Michael Saylor and Phong Le yesterday was one of the most revealing discussions I have seen.

And actually it couldn't have come at a better time considering the recent market dynamics.

My full thoughts below on what stood out to me.

1. Digital Credit Is The Business Model

Saylor made it explicitly clear that creating Digital Credit is central to Strategy's business model.

"The number one way that the company creates shareholder value is to issue good credit."

By issuing Digital Credit and investing the proceeds in $BTC, Strategy can capture the spread between its Cost Of Credit and Bitcoin's appreciation.

The more efficiently Strategy can issue Digital Credit, the greater the economic spread it can capture.

And the more successfully it can scale that model, the more value it will create for common shareholders.

2. $STRC Buybacks Are About Building Trust

Saylor emphasised that supporting Digital Credit during difficult market conditions is essential to building long-term customer confidence.

"People judge you based upon how you treat them in difficult markets."

This reinforces something I have been arguing for months.

Supporting $STRC through buybacks demonstrates Strategy's commitment to its customers.

Management explicitly discussed the downstream implications of this approach, including stronger investor confidence.

In turn, that confidence will attract more durable investors, improve liquidity and ultimately increase Strategy's capacity to issue Digital Credit.

Saylor also acknowledged that decisions which appear less profitable in the short term can become considerably more valuable in the long-term.

For reasons I have explained many times elsewhere, I believe management is making the right decision by prioritising the long-term success of the product over short-term financial optimisation.

3. Product Quality Over Short-Term Growth

Saylor acknowledged that higher dividend rates could stimulate additional demand for $STRC, but explicitly rejected pursuing growth at the expense of common shareholders.

"There might very well be more demand for this if we were paying 15% or 20% than 12%...We just don't wish to do that."

His reasoning was straightforward.

Raising the dividend would increase Strategy's Cost Of Credit and reduce the economic spread available to $MSTR shareholders.

As Saylor put it:

"We're playing the long game."

Instead, Strategy is prioritising price stability, liquidity and investor confidence.

Again, I strongly agree with this approach.

Higher dividend rates may attract incremental demand, but they won't necessarily attract the type of durable institutional investors Strategy is targeting.

And increasing the Cost Of Credit ultimately comes at the expense of common shareholders.

4. $STRC Supply Will Adjust To Demand

Saylor explained that Strategy intends to continuously adjust outstanding $STRC supply according to organic demand rather than pursue issuance growth at any cost.

He estimates that the current level of organic demand for $STRC at a 12% dividend is approximately $5B–$7.5B.

I have no real view on how accurate those numbers are likely to turn out to be. If anything, I would lean lower.

To date, Strategy has repurchased ~$3B of $STRC below par.

Per Saylor, the objective is to establish an equilibrium where buyers and sellers balance around par.

This is something I have consistently advocated.

Maximise the proportion of holders who genuinely want the product for what it is at the minimum sustainable dividend rate.

That establishes a stable foundation upon which future growth can compound.

5. Capital Allocation Is Dynamic

Saylor explained that Strategy evaluates capital allocation opportunities across Bitcoin, common equity, Digital Credit and cash on an ongoing basis.

"We can buy or sell dollars, buy or sell Bitcoin, buy or sell MSTR common stock, buy or sell STRC."

Crucial

posts.text:
The Irrationality of the Rises Was Proportional to the Falls but the Fundamentals Tell a Different Story

The spectacular run-ups in the Neocloud names (CoreWeave, Nebius, and IREN) earlier in 2026 were undeniably euphoric and, in hindsight, irrationally extended. What is equally irrational is the severity of the subsequent collapses.

From their 2026 highs, these stocks have fallen roughly 68–80%. Yet this is not a case of growth stories that stalled or decelerated. On the contrary, all three companies continued to report astronomical revenue growth with no meaningful slowdown:

$CRWV CoreWeave’s quarterly revenue jumped dramatically year-over-year, with a rapidly expanding backlog of contracted AI compute demand.

$NBIS Nebius maintained aggressive capacity expansion and strong sequential growth.

$IREN IREN scaled its AI cloud revenue sharply while building a multi-billion-dollar contracted backlog.

In normal markets, such sustained, high-velocity growth would provide a floor under valuations. Instead, the stocks have been punished as if the growth engine itself had broken. These drawdowns appear driven more by pure speculative sentiment, risk-off positioning, and concerns over leverage and execution timing than by any fundamental deterioration in demand or results.

When companies are still delivering the kind of explosive, non-decelerating growth that justified the earlier enthusiasm, declines of this magnitude are difficult to reconcile with the underlying business performance. The rises were excessive and so, it seems, are the falls.

DYOR

- Browse the web, run commands and write or debug code
- Plan and execute multistep tasks across apps and services
- Coordinate multiple specialized AI agents

Apple has considered launching the service as early as late 2027, though development is still in its early stages.

Meanwhile, Apple is tightening permissions for competing AI agents on Macs. In macOS 27.3, enabling ChatGPT's computer-use capabilities now requires 14 steps, up from four previously, according to Bloomberg.

$ANT ANT IS HEAVY, AND SOME OF THE SHORTS ARE PROBABLY THE OWNERS

Anthropic debuted today into the weakest tape of the year for the AI complex, and the stock has been under pressure from the open. The easy read is that the market is rejecting the valuation. There is a mechanical explanation that fits better, and it starts with who owned this company before today.

Anthropic's cap table is not only institutions. Across years of private rounds, secondary sales and SPVs, a long tail of private individual investors holds pre-IPO stock, in many cases sitting on windfalls of ten to fifty times their money. As of this morning those windfalls are marked to market, and most of them cannot be sold. The lockup runs up to a full year.

A holder in that position has an obvious trade available: short the listed stock against the locked shares, or buy puts once options list, and the paper windfall becomes a locked gain whatever the next year brings. Every point the stock falls from here pays out on the hedge against shares the holder cannot sell until 2027.

Three frictions stand in the way, and they explain why this is pressure rather than a flood. The lockup bars hedging until day 195, June 1, 2027, and then allows only 20% of a holder's remaining restricted shares. A short against the box is a constructive sale for tax purposes, so the gain is taxed as if it were realized. And borrow in a float of about 7% is scarce, expensive and recallable.

But detection is not one of the frictions. Short interest is published twice a month as a single aggregate number with no names attached. No filing identifies a small holder's short. The company and the underwriters, the parties to the lockup, have no window into anyone's brokerage account. For thousands of small private holders, nobody would know.

So some of the early short interest in this name will not be bears betting against Anthropic. It will be owners insuring windfalls they are not allowed to sell. The footprints to watch are the first published short interest print in mid-December, the put skew once ANT options list, and the release dates below, starting December 15, which test how much eligible stock actually gets sold by holders who could not hedge.

The reason the incentive lasts is the schedule itself. Here it is in full.

THE LOCKUP THAT CREATES THE INCENTIVE

Anthropic priced at $83 with about 980M shares in public hands, roughly 7% of the 13.09B shares outstanding. Behind that float sit about 15.5B restricted shares, options and awards, and they do not free up on one date. The prospectus sets 23 release dates across a full year, keyed partly to fixed day counts and partly to earnings reports. Every figure below is an eligibility ceiling. The filing does not say any holder intends to sell.

THE TWO TRACKS

About 2.7B shares, held by employees, non-founder directors and officers, and a group of other stockholders, are restricted for up to 180 days, ending at the earlier of two trading days after Q1 2027 results or May 17, 2027.

About 8.0B shares, held by the seven co-founders and the larger stockholders above 0.5%, are restricted for up to 365 days, ending at the earlier of two trading days after Q3 2027 results or November 18, 2027.

THE RELEASE CALENDAR

Day one, November 19, 2026: up to 316M shares, the non-founder insiders' 10% allowance. The CFO and chief accounting officer are named in the filing as eligible to sell from the first session.

December 15, 2026 and January 5, 2027: up to 299M on each date. 914M cumulative.

posts.name: Jonah Lupton
posts.text:
Over the past couple weeks we've met with management teams across memory, optics, neoclouds, semis, semi cap equipment and substrates.

Everyone is frustrated and confused about their stock prices but everyone is still very, very bullish.

Everyone expects 2027 capex to be significantly higher than 2026 and they expect 2028 capex to be moderately to significantly higher than 2027. 

Everyone knows the YoY capex growth rates will decelerate but the total dollars spent will continue to get bigger... at least for the next few years. Everyone says we're still in the early innings of ai adoption. 

Every company in the ai ecosystem is 50-100% sold out for 2027 and 40-80% sold out for 2028. 

Everyone is sitting on LTAs from the hyperscalers... some of those LTAs are getting signed and they last anywhere from 3 years to 6+ years... and they're getting done at record prices and record margins. Customers can't take the chance of not having enough supply to meet their needs over the next 3-5 years... locking up supply at record prices is better than not having enough supply when it's needed the most. 

Some of these LTAs could consume more than 50% of their supply over the next 2-3 years and at least one company has an LTA that would consume 75% of their capacity over the next 2-3 years. 

Neoclouds continue to see demand that is 5-10x higher than capacity. Many of them are saying the financing concerns are overblown. They're seeing 3-5 year deals get signed at 10-20% higher prices that the first half of 2026 and they think deals signed in the first half of 2027 will have 10-20% higher prices than deals signed in the second half of 2026. Power is still a big bottleneck and many sites are dealing with small construction delays but nothing is getting canceled. Customers are desperate for compute. Many of the neoclouds are trying to reserve 10-15% of capacity for shorter term deals and spot market because rates are 2-3x higher than the 3-5 year deals. 

Memory companies say demand will outstrip supply until 2029 at the earliest. They are very confident LTAs won't get cancelled because even at record prices for memory, the customers have enough margin to make it work. 

I know there's lots of fear and uncertainty in the market right now but it's not showing up in the demand... it remains stronger than ever... many backlogs are growing faster than current revenues.

In 20+ years of investing, I've honestly never seen this much dislocation between fundamentals and valuations. This is truly a historic time to be an investor and not in a good way. It's very hard to be patient and lean into your conviction/thesis during times like this but that's probably the right strategy for most long-term investors. 

Hopefully the lows are near. Make sure you are getting sleep, sunlight and exercise. Protect your mental health if possible.

posts.name: Michael A. Arouet
posts.text:
Peter has a good point. But there is no such thing as “stocks.” There are sectors and individual stocks. Today feels similar to 2000/2001 after the dotcom bubble burst. Companies based on hype, hope, and “this time is different” cratered, while boring “old economy” stocks began a phenomenal bull run.

AI is the future, no doubt about that, but are multi-trillion-dollar valuations justified by expected profits and cash flows? Probably for some, surely not for everyone. As in 1999/2000, some dotcom companies became giants while most disappeared. The problem was that literally all of them were priced to become giants.

Look at data center and semiconductor sector valuations. If Elon is just directionally correct about almost free, unlimited space compute power, most conventional data center companies will go to zero, same for semis. And we all know one should never underestimate Elon.

It starts to feel like a déjà vu, hyped darlings crater while boring consumer staples and healthcare companies hit record heights. Most investors don’t remember 2000, many weren’t even born. Time will tell, human nature doesn’t change, just the hyped darlings do.

quoted.text: There’s no doubt that if the stock market keeps falling, the Fed will pivot, but will that be enough to save stocks? Not necessarily. The Fed cut rates 11 times in 2001, taking the Fed funds rate down from 6.5% to 1.75%. Stocks still fell. I expect the S&P 500 to bounce back into year-end but then fall again in 2027.

How Jack Dorsey remade Block for AI. His logic is that at a remote-first company every interaction leaves "some sort of written artifact," and AI makes all of it searchable by anyone.

Block has only three roles and no middle management:

▫️Individual contributor (IC): builds or operates something ▫️Directly responsible individual (DRI): owns the strategy and roadmap ▫️Coach: individual attached to an IC or DRI to "help them master their craft"

So the middle layer that used to pass information up and down isn't needed: "The chain of command and the communication hierarchy were just slowing a bunch of that information down."

🦔SpaceX just sold $32 billion of debt to buy Nvidia chips it will rent out to AI companies, mostly at interest rates above 8%. Its notes in June averaged under 6%. Anthropic, the IPO everyone cheered on Wednesday night, accounts for about a third of SpaceX’s revenue.

My Take
SpaceX has to keep making about five years of lease payments on these chips, even if the chips themselves fail. Anthropic can walk away on 90 days’ notice. That kind of mismatch works fine while AI companies fight over computing power and gets ugly fast if they stop, and lenders clearly see it, since they charged SpaceX almost 2.5 points more than they did five months ago. With Anthropic down about 13% today and Nvidia down about 7%, the tenant and the chip supplier are both falling at the same time as the landlord.

posts.name: Damnang
posts.text:
I grabbed a bite with my friend from NVIDIA again yesterday. They’d listened in on the earnings call and said management tried to lift the mood right from the start.

One of the first things employees heard at the staff meeting the next day was that they’d get their performance ratings and find out the size of their stock grants in December. They’d expected to wait until next March for that news. I’d been wondering what the press meant by a “bonus,” since NVIDIA engineers don’t typically get an annual cash bonus. My friend said it meant larger RSU refreshers this time around.

My friend also told me about a question someone asked Jonah Alben, NVIDIA’s senior vice president of GPU engineering, at a meeting with their whole team. The employee said several outside recruiters had been reaching out pretty aggressively and asked whether NVIDIA had a plan to keep people from being poached.

The answer was about what you’d expect. But hearing that someone had asked the question gave me a sense of just how much attention NVIDIA’s senior engineers are getting from recruiters, especially those at the director level and above. People with that kind of experience are hard to find in Silicon Valley right now.

My friend is worried Jensen Huang might not come back. They wonder what the next few years will look like for NVIDIA. They only joined recently, but they said a lot of the excitement they felt when they took the job is already gone.

NVIDIA offered them less in total compensation than its competitors did. They chose NVIDIA anyway because they believed in Jensen and in the company’s future under him. Yesterday they told me they regret that decision. I tried to reassure them and told them I thought things would get better….

posts.name: Aidan Mackenzie
posts.text:
The Senate passing permitting is absolutely historic! Let's take a second to remember how long folks have been trying to get major permitting & transmission reforms: 🧵

For 50 years presidents have been frustrated by slow permitting and wanted to expand the grid. But for decades environmental and utility opposition made reform impossible

– 1971: Nixon asked Congress to reform transmission. But Congress never voted on the proposal (environmental and state's rights concerns blocked it)

– 1979: President Carter tried to get reforms to speed up energy approvals and judicial review to fix "endless roadblocks." Environmentalists opposed and the bill died in the House in 1980

– 2001: President Bush sought reforms for transmission developers to acquire land (Congress delayed until 2005)

– 2005: Following a massive blackout in 2003, Congress finally acted to boost grid development In the Energy Policy Act of 2005. However, the bill was change to add language that undercut the federal backstop for transmission (the process never built any lines)

– 2009: Obama asked Congress to facilitate building out the grid but Congress's proposal to give FERC siting authority never passed (utilities and environmental groups opposed)

– 2011: After permitting slowed economic recovery projects Obama said "Shovel-ready was not as shovel-ready as we expected"

– 2011-2024: FERC attempted to act to facilitate new interregional lines. However, FERC Order 1000 has failed to produce even a single line

– 2015: Congress passed the FAST Act, which created FAST-41. But Congress declined to add major reforms to judicial review or touch the underlying permitting laws

– 2018: Trump's request to limit reviews to 2 years was never taken up by Congress

– 2022: Despite ongoing delays to infrastructure and climate projects, the Senate voted down the Manchin-Biden-Schumer permitting reform & transmission proposal (Opposition from environmentalists and transmission opponents)

– 2023: Congress declined to include major reforms in the Fiscal Responsibility Act (added only very minor changes)

– 2024: The Manchin-Barrasso bipartisan permitting & transmission bill never got a floor vote

The reforms in BAAJA are transformative and historic. This Congress is on the cusp of reform that has been impassive for over 50 years

posts.text:
There is real fear that Nvidia might pull back on their investments and backstops. 
 
I believe this is misplaced. Nvidia’s competitors are eager to take their place, disrupt their relationships and fill any vacuum left by Nvidia.
 
There are at least three companies aggressively vying to be the new “Central Bank” of AI.
 
Across many @atreidesmgmt venture portfolio companies we are seeing Nvidia’s semiconductor and hyperscale competitors trying to lean in and displace Nvidia in important relationships. Ironically, sometimes at more favorable terms than those offered by Nvidia.
 
And of course, also beginning to see the first signs of Nvidia waking up to this risk and addressing it. Their strategic imperatives have not changed and their strategy was sound, but there is only one Jensen and competitors are now attempting to really take advantage of his absence. No one wants a monopsony at the lab layer.
 
I suspect the same thing is happening in the supply chain. But again, there is only one Jensen.

posts.text:
Cathie Wood calls SpaceX a sleeper AI-model winner, pulling away from the pack with Anthropic and OpenAI

“Well, it’s very interesting. So you’re talking about the Pareto frontier, which is price for a price-performance, or price given level of intelligence. And what we’re seeing is, yes, Anthropic has the leading edge of the Pareto frontier. If you look beyond that, what you’ll find is that OpenAI is dominating the rest of the Pareto frontier, which is really important now that enterprises are thinking about ways to bring more efficiency into their AI spending.”

“And in fact, the Chinese models are not up at the Pareto frontier. I don’t think many people understand that. So I would put another company not too far behind. I think it’s a sleeper, and that’s SpaceX SI. And I think the name of the game here is computing power and energy, or power. And I think these three companies have a preferred position out there, one way or the other. Elon’s creating it himself with orbital data centers, ultimately. But I think that they are pulling away from the pack.”

quoted.text:
Cathie Wood predicts SpaceX’s orbital compute will become cheaper than terrestrial compute within two years, and says last weekend’s Starship catch was critical to that call

posts.name: SemiAnalysis
posts.text: This conference season, Ayar Labs put real manufacturing statistics on its SuperNova ELSFPs. More than 100 laser units were measured at 50 C with -20 dB back reflections to simulate imperfections in fiber connectors and fiber-to-PIC coupling. The notable stats include a mean RIN of -158 dB/Hz and an especially low mean linewidth of 0.16 MHz, comparable to what 400ZR coherent class lasers are specified at; giving a lot of margin for DWDM operation. Importantly, every laser met spec with margin, which matters a lot more in production than one device achieving extraordinary performance.

posts.text:
Scott Bessent says the U.S. has curtailed China’s remote access to overseas compute, because restricting chip sales makes no sense if the same chips can be rented abroad

EISEN: “The new policy you worked on, Treasury and the National Security Council cracking down on overseas data centers that rent significant computing power to China without the chips entering China. Was that aimed at the MegaSpeed revelations?”

BESSENT: “There are two things there, Sarah. One is the ability of companies to violate U.S. policy and sell chips to China. The other is a more common-sense approach we’ve taken on remote access. It doesn’t make any sense not to sell the chips when they could be leased out from overseas data centers.”

EISEN: “Is there a dispute within the administration, between you and Secretary Lutnick, over how aggressive to be in cutting off these chips to China?”

BESSENT: “I think we’re all committed to following President Trump’s instructions... We are going to see that the proper chip restrictions are in place, and the remote access has been curtailed. The U.S. has a substantial lead in our chip technology, and from that lead we are able to maintain our substantial lead with our superintelligence frontier labs.”

quoted.text:
Scott Bessent reveals Jensen Huang did not come up in China talks at all, and says he expects no change to Nvidia’s H200 export policy for China

EISEN: “Did Jensen Huang come up in any of your discussions with the Chinese?”

BESSENT: “No.”

EISEN: “Not at all. Nothing about the spy allegations? Did they ask you to keep the sales of the H200 chips open?”

BESSENT: “Well, we’ve already agreed that the H200s are the threshold level of chips that could be sold to the Chinese, and that continues as planned, and everything beneath there.”

EISEN: “This week in earnings, NVIDIA said it stopped shipping H200s to China even though it had the U.S. licenses and approval to do so. So I was wondering if the administration asked NVIDIA to stop, or if there’s going to be any change in this policy.”

BESSENT: “I wouldn’t anticipate any change in the policy. President Trump was very clear when he made the policy. He drew a very firm line at the H200s, and believes that is the level that China should be able to get. I think what we have seen is a paucity of orders from the Chinese on the H200s, as they try to build out their own chip stack, and I think that they are probably many years behind.”

posts.name: Peter Schiff
posts.text:
In 2008, gold sold off before the worst of the stock market crash. Following a 30% decline, gold bottomed in October, but stocks kept falling until March 2009, with the S&P down nearly 60%. From its 2008 bottom to its 2011 peak, gold surged 166% to nearly double its 2008 high, while the S&P remained well below its 2007 high.

I believe the coming financial crisis will be much worse, and gold's ultimate gain much greater. Just like in 2008, gold is again falling first, but stocks will ultimately fall much further. They’ll keep falling after gold reverses, and gold will soar to new record highs while stocks remain far below their old highs.

posts.name: Markets & Mayhem
posts.text:
The co-founder of the first humanoid company on the Nasdaq says he can’t love his own robot.

Jonathan Hurst wrote that 17 days before Agility Robotics listed.

Digit 5 is the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot the company will ever build, and it can no longer run or jump. It “feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build.”

Much of the weight is the safety system. To work outside a cage, Digit 5 stops, sets its load down, sits on the floor and cuts power when a person gets close.

Hurst’s own read is the useful part. Customers didn’t ruin his vision, they showed him what it was missing.

He goes one step further. If a humanoid looks like a person and works a full warehouse shift, it either can’t lift the weight or can’t last the shift. If it isn’t covered in sensors, it isn’t safe to stand next to.

That’s the diligence question for the category. RoboStrategy’s Scott Walter puts most of Agility’s future on $300 million of orders for 1,000 robots, all from one customer who is also an investor. It pays only if Digit 5 ships on schedule and passes safety certification.

First to market is a label. Shipping is the business.

quoted.text:
WHAT ARE INVESTORS ACTUALLY BUYING WHEN THEY BUY AGILITY ROBOTICS?

Scott Walter, Robotics Research Diligence Director at RoboStrategy, gives his take in the full interview

He says it's still an early-stage company that raced to market through a SPAC. At around 14 times 2025 revenue, he says you're buying the future, not the present.

His advice is to put the "first pure-play humanoid" label aside and do your due diligence on Digit 5, the robot he says the company's future rests on.

He also explains why he thinks humanoids could do a majority of physical work within five years, and why the robots don't have to do everything to be useful. They just have to do enough that someone is willing to pay for that work.

posts.text:
Pinterest, Spotify and Etsy are increasingly emphasizing human “taste” as a competitive edge. Some recent examples: 

Spotify co-CEO Gustav Söderström in Q1 2026 earnings call: 

“Some of the things in the world are facts that can be easily commoditized by LLMs, [such as the capital of Texas]. Other things are not so easily commoditized. And it turns out luckily for us, taste is not easily commoditized because it's not a fact, it's an opinion.

It differs between people, it differs between regions, it differs between people in those regions and use cases. And on top of that, it changes weekly…So, for this reason, we do invest quite a lot in something like our large personalization model, basically our own taste model.”

Pinterest CEO Bill Ready in Q2 2026 earnings call: 

“Our scale and the unique human curation that occurs on our platform have fueled our proprietary Taste Graph, with more than 80 billion monthly searches on Pinterest. 

The vast majority of searches are visual, and over half are commercial. There are also more than 16 billion boards created on our platform. We have a uniquely valuable signal of human taste and curation at scale. 

This enables us to train our AI with a deep understanding of taste, context, and intent that gets more personalized every time a user comes back. This powerful feedback loop is what helps users discover what they want before they have the exact words, brand, or product in mind. That’s why so many commercial journeys begin on Pinterest.”

Etsy CEO Kruti Patel Goyal in Q3 2026 shareholder letter: 

“Etsy’s challenge has never been a lack of choice - it's helping each shopper find what's uniquely right for them. With rich and expanding data on both our buyers and our inventory, we’re well positioned to build on-site shopping assistants that understand buyers' tastes and intent more deeply and connect them with the right items in even more powerful ways than off-site agents.”

Our on-demand GPU rental indices publish a set of prices. We try to be as exhaustive and rigorous as possible to capture the GPU on-demand market accurately. On-demand prices are surging. Econ 101 says that means demand is rising relative to supply for on-demand compute. 

What these prices cannot tell you are the sources of demand or the "quality of demand", whether the demand for compute had come from a long-term sustainable organic source. 

Combined with our term/forward curves, our data provide but one set of data points in a multi-dimensional and multifacted market that's the markets for compute. To get a full read, esp for the implications for the stocks of AI value chain, other data points will have to come to bear too.

quoted.text:
And “all the dollars” in the world are available for the taking if “super intelligence” is willing to pay for it (well up to a point). What’s the highest level of (risk-free) interest rate that’s still consistent with an aggressive AI buildout offering a solid return and positive net PV?

The point @chamath was making in the clip @elonmusk responded to was that in order to raise more capital (dollars) to build out AI, Anthropic likely would have to concede a substantial amount of equity valuation, which is just the flip side of expected equity returns. 

More dollars are always available for the taking for super intelligence as long as higher rates of returns are promised either in the form of higher interest rates (debt) or higher equity returns (lower stock prices). In some grand sense, Modigliani-Miller theorem holds. 

Finally, all of the above is true up to a point, which is “credit rationing” due to adverse selection. At some point, someone borrows so much money and/or at such a high interest rates that the lenders’ natural assumption leans towards that the borrowers may be strategically intending on defaulting. That that’s the only way to justify their borrowing.

posts.name: Puru Saxena
posts.text:
Lots of posts on X that this is 2000, 2008 or 2022.   

At this stage, its not conclusive that we are in a lengthy bear-market. Even those bear-markets had face ripping multi-week rallies and in terms of positioning and sentiment we are very washed out now.

The TMT bust (2000-2002) was triggered by tight monetary which inverted the yield curve and caused a recession. Back then, the NASDAQ also traded at an absurd valuation. Today, the yield curve is not inverted and the NASDAQ's forward PE is at the same level as the COVID-crash low!

The 2008 bust was triggered by the housing bubble and the collapse of various banks; which is not the case today. 

The 2022 bear market was triggered by the Federal Reserve which abruptly ended massive QE and embarked on a severe rate hiking cycle. This is also not similar with the current situation. 

This time around, the market is worrying about a slowdown in AI capex for 2028 and beyond; and uncertainty surrounding Nvidia's leadership and circular financing arrangements. In spring the market was also very worried about AI killing cybersecurity and infrastructure software companies and that turned out to be dead wrong. 

The jury is still out on how the Dems sweep will impact the AI capex cycle and how Nvidia's next CEO will manage the business. During times like these when most are super bearish and sentiment is super negative, best to remain calm and focus on the facts.

A few people have asked what I’m doing right now. Honestly, very little. I only own four stocks, and all I’m really doing is moving money between those four. I do use stop losses to manage my portfolio. Sometimes I cancel them and add them back. A 10% drop doesn’t really bother me. I use them to help limit the damage from a much sharper drop.

I like holding high-beta stocks, so I expect sell-offs like this. I’ve also seen how quickly the gains can come. If I remember right, I was down around 50% YTD in April 2025. From there, I needed a 100% gain just to break even, and I ended the year up over 400%. That’s how volatile my portfolio can be.

This year alone, I’ve seen my portfolio swing by six figures in a month. At one point I was up around 80% YTD. I didn’t take much profit because I had a target in mind for how much I wanted to grow the portfolio. I started it to pay off my 25-year mortgage in 10 years. If it takes 15 years, so be it. I have that flexibility.

I’ve done my research on the four companies I hold, and overall I’m happy with their progress. One is more of a short-term position. Of the long-term holdings, the one I’m watching closely is the subscription business. I’ve always said that if subscriber numbers started falling, I’d start to question my thesis. That’s the one where I’m getting close. I’m comfortable with the others.

Right now, I’m trying to do as little as possible. I’ll keep moving money between my four holdings when it makes sense, but unless something drastic happens, I don’t plan to add any new money to the account this year. I’m more focused on 2027 now.

posts.name: Jeffrey Currie 🆔++
posts.text:
My first appearance on @KitcoNewsNOW comes amidst a sell-off on gold and other precious metals. 

@JeremySzafron  asked me where I stand on gold at the moment and whilst I said I was cautious, it's not because of gold itself, but because of the wider liquidity squeeze that is emerging.

Gold is a hedge against a longer-term solvency crisis, not an immediate liquidity squeeze. When dollars become scarce, investors sell what they can to raise cash, and gold happens to be one of the easiest assets to liquidate.

Remember what I said on @business last week about the two boogeymen of commodities - scarcity and debasement: Scarcity is the fear of running out of the commodity. Debasement is the fear of running out of money.

Pair that with the issuance of debt from costly data centre build-outs, issues with NASDAQ and the equity sell-off, a looming interest rate hike, and you've got a huge demand for dollars at a time when supply is decreasing. It has created the perfect storm to release gold, copper and other hard assets to raise cash.

So, where gold is currently susceptible to dollar liquidity, oil is a different story, and it all comes down to economics of storing inventories.

With industrial metals, storage is relatively cheap. You need a physical location, a chain-link fence and a guard dog. You can stack inventories to the moon if you wanted to - the point is, it much easier to build up stocks and liquidate them when you need to raise cash.

The same doesn't apply to oil: storing large volumes of oil requires expensive infrastructure and carrying costs. You can't store quantities of oil as you would gold on anywhere near the same scale.

The bottom line: Dollar liquidity pressures can drive selling across the market, but oil is far less exposed to liquidity dynamics - and crucially, those dynamics do not make the physical cost of delivering said oil any cheaper.

My interview in full will be release shortly, so stay tuned for that - a great discussion with Jeremy, thank you for having me on.

That’s probably the most important chart for Europe’s future. Europe’s near-total absence from frontier AI is the not surprising outcome of choices that systematically raise costs and slow the building and scaling of advanced models. The main constraint is regulation. The AI Act, layered on GDPR and national rules, adds months or years of delay and millions in compliance costs before a model can even be released.

While the US and China race to train and deploy, European teams spend time on paperwork. The result is clear in competitive models, just one European effort versus dozens from the US and China. Capital and talent follow the same pattern. Europe’s venture ecosystem remains smaller and more risk-averse. Top researchers frequently leave for labs offering better resources and fewer procedural hurdles. Energy prices, elevated by policies that reduced baseload capacity, further raise the enormous cost of training runs. Fragmentation across 27 legal systems multiplies every friction.

Competitiveness consequences are severe. Most high-value software, industrial automation, drug discovery, logistics, and customer-facing services will increasingly embed frontier models. European firms unable to train or fine-tune at the frontier will license American or Chinese systems, transferring value and strategic leverage abroad, or offer less capable products. Over time this erodes margins, slows productivity growth, and hinders retention of remaining technical talent. In dual-use domains, dependence creates geopolitical exposure, access can be restricted, pricing raised, or capabilities withheld.

Catch-up is still possible but requires reversing current incentives rather than adding regulations. Without that shift, Europe’s industrial and services base will operate one generation behind the systems defining the next productivity wave. Europe decimated its legacy industry with its energy approach and runs a serious risk of finishing off its remaining industry by choosing bureaucracy over AI advancement. Can you imagine the consequences for Europe's prosperity, standard of living, and geopolitical security?

posts.name: Patrick Moorhead
posts.text: Azure Cobalt tested.

quoted.text:
Signal65 compared the latest @Azure Cobalt 200 with Cobalt 100, two generations of the custom Arm-based server processor from Microsoft, across four kinds of work.

We ran both generations on the largest general-purpose VM of each and reported results per instance and per vCPU. The Cobalt 200 VM has 1.33x the vCPUs, so the per-vCPU view shows how much of the gain comes from each core. The report also includes EDA chip-design results that Microsoft silicon engineers produced on their own design flows, which Signal65 reviewed.

Key findings from the Lab Insight:

➡️ Cobalt 200 delivered 1.43x to 5.53x the throughput of Cobalt 100 per instance, and 1.07x to 4.15x per vCPU

➡️ Developer and system tasks ran at 1.76x the work per instance on Terminal-Bench 2 in our testing

➡️ Function calling for AI agents reached 1.59x to 1.93x the requests per second per instance, with identical accuracy

➡️ GROMACS molecular dynamics rose 1.43x to 1.46x per instance

➡️ RTL simulation for chip design completed 3.43x to 5.53x the jobs per hour per instance, in tests run by Microsoft silicon engineers and reviewed by Signal65

➡️ A fleet sized for a fixed load needs roughly 30% to 48% fewer instances on the developer, agentic AI and HPC workloads we tested

Read the full Lab Insight: https://signal65.com/research/azure-cobalt-200-outperforms-cobalt-100-per-instance-and-per-core/

CHINA 🇨🇳 SEEKS TO RESTART U.S. PRIVATE EQUITY INVESTMENTS: FT

China's sovereign wealth fund, China Investment Corporation, is negotiating terms with private equity firms that would allow Chinese investors to recover their money if U.S. or European sanctions are imposed, without forcing funds to sell their assets.

Proposals include repayment arrangements tied to fund exits, separate investment vehicles and provisions allowing investors to opt out of individual deals.

Chinese state-backed investors stopped making new U.S. private equity commitments during last year's trade war, after previously backing firms including Blackstone, Carlyle, Thoma Bravo and Vista Equity.

Fund advisers say Trump's recent China visit helped revive CIC's interest, although no new investment commitments have been announced.

Poland’s post-1989 economic transformation remains an unbelievable success, a shift from a poor socialist economy to a large, export-oriented market that has approached Western living standards, surpassed $1 trillion in GDP, and often outpaced most of the EU. Extending this model further without friction is less certain though. Let’s take a look:

Demographics pose the most immediate pressure. Fertility is at postwar lows, natural population decline is routine, and the core working-age population is set to shrink by over a million within a decade. Immigration and higher older-worker participation help but do not fully offset the loss. Fewer workers supporting more retirees means slower potential growth, tighter labor markets, and rising pressure on pensions and healthcare. A move to higher retirement age, especially for women, is needed.

Fiscal space is narrowing. Deficits near 7 percent of GDP stem partly from elevated defense spending and resistance to consolidation before the 2027 elections. Rising debt, more cautious rating agencies, and the government-presidency standoff hinder corrective measures. High borrowing costs and limited counter-cyclical room leave the country more exposed to shocks.

每当市场大跌的时候，这种宝典文章都是穿越时空的投资者指南。

如何战胜股市波动的投资者指南

3根阴线改变信仰，预测难执行更难。既然未来不可测波动加大，投资者怎么办？

6月1日上海两千多万人从 Covid 封控中走出来的日子。如果在 2020 年初，有人告诉你，一座中国最国际化的大都市会经历那样的封控、停摆和集体记忆，你会信吗？（订阅者专享｜周报深度 5/31的公开版 他强任他强：尾部事件冲击下的六月买方策略）

这就是尾部事件。

不是因为它一定没人想到，而是因为人在趋势中，总是高估眼前秩序的稳定性，低估极端拐点对现实世界的冲击。
市场也一样。

人类擅长把最近发生的事情外推成未来，却不擅长理解真正的结构性跳变。半导体存储就是例子。2023 年 DRAM 和 NAND 还在周期低谷，市场规模不到千亿美元级别，到了 2026、2027 年，AI 需求和价格周期把整个行业重新推到完全不同的量级。你让分析师在低谷线性预测十倍变化，很多模型都没有意义。

所以本周的标题是金庸那句话：

他强任他强，清风拂山岗。

外部越乱，越要有自己的内在秩序。

但这里的“坚定”，不是无脑 all in，不是喊口号，也不是抱着一个股票谈恋爱。真正的坚定，来自你知道自己该看什么，知道什么变量在改变，知道什么价格已经包含了什么预期，知道仓位该如何承受尾部事件冲击。

核心就看三件事：
分子、分母、仓位纪律。

posts.text:
Bending Spoons just bought Mailchimp for $3.68 billion. Intuit paid $12 billion for it in 2021.

Mailchimp actually got the best price of the five big names Bending Spoons has bought, measured against each one’s peak valuation:

- Miro: $17.5B peak (Jan 2022). Sold for about $1.79B. 10 cents on the dollar.
- Vimeo: $7.2B at its 2021 spin-off. Sold for $1.38B. 19 cents.
- Airtable: $11B peak (Dec 2021). Sold for about $2.25B. 20 cents.
- Eventbrite: $1.76B at its 2018 IPO. Sold for $500M. 28 cents.
- Mailchimp: $12B in 2021. Sold for $3.68B. 31 cents.

None of these companies were DOA. They’re big, well-known, mostly recurring businesses with millions of customers. They stopped growing, and in 2026 a big B2B company that isn’t growing sells for 2-3x revenue.

Mailchimp is guiding to 0% growth this year on about $1.26B of revenue. In 2021 it was growing 20% on $800M, which is how it got 15x.

A crash from near the highs

A fast rebound

Several quiet sessions on light volume

A second breakdown on rising volume

The closest price paths failed the test because none contained a 4% to 6% crash on three times normal volume.

This pattern is genuinely rare.

So we changed the question.

What historically happened when SPY:

Fell at least 3.5% on twice normal volume

Rebounded

Closed below the crash-day close within 5 to 15 sessions

Only six prior episodes qualified.

Twenty sessions after the breakdown:
SPY average: -5.6%
SPY median: -2.2%
QQQ average: -4.3%

Four of six SPY cases finished lower.

Compared with randomly selected high-volatility periods, the SPY result produced a resampled p-value of 0.041. QQQ produced p = 0.067.

2007 and 2025: the breakdown was the low or close to it.

The 60-session result offered no reliable edge:

SPY median: +5.3%

Positive cases: four of six

The most relevant comparison may be 2007.

posts.name: Diane Swonk
posts.text:
Sitting on a One-Legged Stool?

The economy bent. It didn’t break. The AI boom and the wealth it generated kept it going, but concentrated gains in the hands of a few firms and households. The result was a resilience that failed to resonate for too many.

Now the AI trade is wobbling and our strength is our vulnerability. It is akin to sitting on a one-legged stool. Alfred Nobel, yes, of Nobel Prize fame, used a one to keep his workers from nodding off while mixing nitroglycerin. 🤯

The same wealth gains that helped sustain consumer spending can become a vulnerability when markets correct. The narrower the source of resilience, the greater the exposure when it weakens. Escalating inequality is both a social and economic liability.

Bubbles and technological innovation have long been uneasy companions. History is littered with them. Canals, railroads, electrification and the tech boom of the 1990s are all examples. 

Investors front-run the promise. Capital floods in. Infrastructure gets built. Innovation can endure, even if the investment boom often doesn’t.

Backlogs are large. Demand hasn’t disappeared. Speculative players will get knocked out along the way.

That’s a shakeout but it does not guarantee a soft landing. My worry is what happens if a correction grows tentacles, moving from equities into credit and ultimately the broader economy.

Then there are the vulnerabilities in the technology itself. The rush to harness AI’s capabilities is being matched by a rush to patch vulnerabilities in our systems.

Necessary? Absolutely. 
Reassuring? Hardly.

Innovation requires technology; productivity growth requires trust, which we are lacking. People need to believe their fortunes will rise with the tide, not recede with the shore.

What plays well in Silicon Valley isn’t sitting well on Main Street. Wall Street is getting uncomfortable, too. That is a lot of weight to put on one leg.

My fear isn’t simply that the AI trade corrects. It is that a correction reveals just how much of the economy’s resilience has come to depend on the wealth and investment the boom created.

Resilience that doesn’t resonate could become a reckoning. It is hard living in my head these days. 
Reupping the link to my bear market scenario. Unclear how much wiggle room the Federal Reserve will have to step in and cut, given tail on backlogs and supply chains problems.

posts.text:
THE COUNT 📌

Today marks the 3rd 80%+ downside breadth day in 11 sessions: Nov 5, Nov 12, and today.

Nov 5 snapped a 243-session streak without one—the longest in at least 30 years. History shows they rarely come alone: in 11 of the 15 prior cases since 1996, at least one more followed within 30 sessions.

Drawdowns from 52-week highs so far:

• Nasdaq: -13.9%

• Dow Jones: -10.3% 

• S&P 500: -8.5% (6-day losing streak)

DISTRIBUTION OR CAPITULATION?
Three 80%+ downside days in a tight cluster point to two paths:

• Capitulation: sellers flush out in waves, answered by an 80–90% UPSIDE breadth day within sessions

• Distribution: weak bounces, lower highs, and continued institutional selling

What leans capitulation:

• Record-negative dealer gamma (forced mechanical selling)

• Stretched oversold readings & heavy hedging demand

What leans distribution:

• Fundamental headwinds (AI capex ROI scrutiny, hawkish Fed 50 bps hike talk, Middle East tensions)

• Broken key support (Dow <50k) lacking dip-buyers

The tell: Watch for an 80–90% upside breadth day over the next few sessions. Without it, bounces remain suspect.

My primary weekly count suggests GLD is working through a larger Wave 4 correction following the completion of Wave 3.

I've currently labeled Wave 4 as an A-B-C zigzag, but that doesn't mean the correction must end in three waves. Wave 4 can develop into a more complex corrective structure, including a combination or triangle.

Jensen out at Nvidia, Anthropic's $1.4T IPO, HubSpot brings back Halligan, and Microsoft 365 down for two days.

#1 Anthropic will hit $100B in revenue with under 6,000 employees

One-person billion-dollar startups and S-tier security can't both be true.

**Closing Brief — Thu Nov 19**

● S&P 500 7,175.83 (-2.02%) — sixth straight down day
● Nasdaq 23,879.20 (-2.25%)
● Dow 49,097.06 (-2.19%, -1,101 pts) — closed below 50,000

**What happened**
● Stocks attempted to rally right out of the gate, but the effort quickly faltered. There really wasn't a lot of incremental news on Thursday specifically, and many of the reasons cited for the pressure could have been said at any time in the last few weeks
● Among the more popular justifications for the ugly price action: 1) a hawkish Fed — the FOMC is guaranteed to hike on 12/9, probably again on 1/27 and maybe 3/17 too, as it tries to wrap its arms around an inflation problem that's worse than anticipated; 2) Iran uncertainty — NYT, Axios and Bloomberg all ran "Trump is considering another bombing campaign" stories, although oil took it in stride and didn't really rally, with global markets in a state of oversupply; 3) continued AI doubts — the Anthropic IPO was impressive, but the overall pool of capital available to finance data centers remains smaller than before, while incremental restrictions on chip sales to China are already having an impact on the industry
● 4) poor economic data — the Philadelphia Fed report pointed to cooling growth and intensifying inflation; 5) US government shutdown risks — a shutdown is possible as soon as 12/11; 6) cybersecurity fears — every day brings a new wave of cyber-attack and IT-outage headlines, and they're starting to weigh on the market; 7) blah retail earnings — WMT was OK with a modest beat-and-raise, but BBWI and WSM each provided cautious guidance for Q4
● Sentiment as of the 4pm close was particularly bleak — SPX below its 200-day and sitting at multi-month lows, most people abandoning hope for a year-end rally. The midterms, Nvidia earnings and Ant's IPO don't appear to have been the clearing events many anticipated, and it's difficult to envision a catalyst to propel a dramatic turnaround, with AI-linked stuff still in the penalty box while defensives are extended and expensive

**Movers**

**Rates / oil**

**Levels**
● SPY $715.87, 8.4% off its $781.62 high — sitting right on the $715 level; QQQ $645.04, 15.4% off its $762.86 high
● SPY levels: $715 (8.5% off highs), $681 (12.8% off), $671 (14.1% off)

posts.name: Alphatica
posts.text:
A market can enter a bottoming process before it prints its final low.

That is exactly what we said on November 5.

We did not guarantee a V-shaped recovery or claim that $732.71 had to hold. In the closest historical profiles, only 20% of SPY lows avoided another lower close during the following 10 sessions.

A retest or marginal undercut was part of the original framework.

A close below $732.71 would invalidate November 5 as the exact price low.

It would not automatically invalidate the broader tactical-bottoming thesis.

That thesis fails if the market sustains a break below the low while new lows expand, breadth deteriorates and liquidation accelerates.

The distinction matters:

An exact bottom is one price.

A bottoming process can take several weeks.

We called the process. The market is still determining the final price.

posts.name: Gina Martin Adams
posts.text:
The security risks uncovered by Jensen Huang's affair and dealings with companies in and around China could further restrict money flows in the sector at large, via regulatory pressures on the industry and export restrictions on its products.  In our Chart of the Week on November 13th, we pointed out that Congress could attempt to tighten export controls given the news that Nvidia chips were illegally making their way to China. Based on publicly filed data, 6% of the company’s revenue could be impacted in such a worst-case scenario. This figure likely understates sales to the country given the possibly illicit nature of the dealings and indirect sales to China through Southeast Asia. Nonetheless, any curtailment of the significant portion of Nvidia’s revenue and subsequently cash flows that comes from China sales might dent company efforts to fund other areas of the AI buildout. 
 
Likewise, tighter export restrictions could have a material impact on overall index, semiconductor, and AI supplier revenues. Currently, a relatively small 2.3 percentage points of S&P 500 revenue growth is expected to come from China in 2027. However, 21.7 and 13.7 percentage points of the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) and AI supplier’s topline growth is forecast to come from China next year. Even if all revenues from China vanished, estimates imply the SOX would still post 29.7% sales growth next year. While this is still extremely robust, it would mark a sharp deceleration from 2026’s 68.6% pace. Removing all disclosed China revenue would likewise drop the S&P 500 and AI suppliers 2027 topline growth rate by roughly 2.3 and 13.7 percentage points, landing them at 6.5% and 29.3% growth respectively, a material slowdown from 13.4% and 66.3% growth in 2026.

For more, see today's Market Sense: "Nvidia's Tangled Web Threatens Slower AI-Build, Pressures Neoclouds"
on http://hbwealth.com

posts.name: Trung Phan
posts.text:
Great chat with Ben and Eric as always.

This part on bull case for Google's AI Mode very interesting:

▫️a good Google search gets you off the platform fast (search, click, leave…fewer clicks better)
▫️chatbots (eg. AI Mode) wants you to stay in the chat and engaged, which creates room for more ads and every extra turn tells Google more about you
▫️Google can drop relevant ads at different points in the chat (able to stack ~10 ads in one conversation vs. one batch per search)
▫️a chat covers the whole marketing funnel (brand ads early then targeted ads later)
▫️the more turns a user does, the pricier the ad gets until conversion

Google re-architecting its ad business on the fly similar to Meta doing it Reels.

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
Productivity, Not Rate Hikes, Tames Supercore!

Supercore inflation is no mystery, and it’s not a story about the federal funds rate. It is unit labor costs: pay minus productivity.

PCE supercore and nonfarm unit labor costs have a correlation of 0.82 since 1960, and 0.91 on two-year averages. In 2022, productivity fell 1.5%, unit labour costs rose 5.3%, and supercore peaked at 5.3% in October. In 2024, productivity rose 3.1% and unit labor  costs slowed to 2.0%, even as pay grew 5.1%. 

Supercore came down. The 1996 to 2004 boom worked the same way: productivity 3.1%, pay 4.4%, unit labor costs 1.3%, supercore 2.6%.

The only extended stretch when supercore held near 2% was post-GFC secular stagnation, from mid-2009 to early 2020. It averaged 2.1% and stayed in a 1.5% to 2.5% band in 82% of months, against 15% otherwise. It got there through weak pay of 2.5%, not a productivity boom.

Supercore has been above 2% in 88% of months since 1960, with a long-run average of 4.05%. It was 3.6% in September 2026. In the third quarter, unit labour costs were 2.4%, productivity 2.1% and pay 4.5%. Rate hikes do not create productivity. They cut the investment, including AI capex, that does.

A Fed that hikes into a productivity boom to chase a 2% supercore it has seen only in secular stagnation is not following the data. It is going rogue. The Fed should protect the productivity cycle, not choke it.
