FED'S COOK CALLS FOR TIGHTER MONETARY POLICY, WARNS INFLATION RISKS ARE GROWING

Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook warned that current interest rates are not restrictive enough to bring inflation under control.

Cook said September's rate hike was insufficient and that delaying further tightening risks embedding inflation, potentially requiring more aggressive action later.

She described financial conditions as too accommodative, while characterizing economic growth as strong and the labor market as healthy.

Her remarks reinforce the case for additional Fed rate hikes.

Paul Tudor Jones: Almost Every Big Crash Has the Same Root Cause, Too Much Leverage Somewhere

If I think of some really, really big accidents, most of them have the same underlying reason, same underlying foundation, which is some too much leverage somewhere. Most of the leverage, most of the time, if I think of the big ones, were derivative inspired, either futures or options.

1987, that crash was 100% portfolio insurance, 100%. Had they had limits, which they didn't, it would have been a 10%, maybe 15% max, but that was 100% derivatives.

If I think about 1998, Long-Term Capital, big derivatives, they had a huge balance sheet with a lot of derivatives they were offsides on.

2000 was a little different. 2000 was the easiest bear market I've ever seen in my whole life. posts.text:
Coup de tonnerre énorme dans les mathématiques

Levent Alpöge, mathématicien chez Anthropic, a publié ce vendredi une note sur son site perso. 

Première phrase : « I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis »

Et il va plus loin dans la note la même méthode réglerait aussi l'hypothèse de Riemann généralisée

Pour l'échelle, elle a été posée par Bernhard Riemann en 1859. Ça fait 167 ans que les plus grands mathématiciens se cassent les dents dessus

Si ça tient, c'est une news énormissime pour le monde des maths. Historique total

1. C'est quoi l'hypothèse de Riemann ?

Les nombres premiers (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13…) ont l'air de tomber au hasard sur la droite des nombres

Riemann a trouvé une fonction, la fonction zêta, qui encode leur répartition. Elle s'annule en une infinité de points, ses « zéros »

L'hypothèse dit que tous les zéros intéressants (les non triviaux) sont alignés sur une seule et même droite, celle où la partie réelle vaut 1/2

En clair : les nombres premiers sont aussi bien rangés qu'ils peuvent l'être. Le désordre apparent cache un ordre quasi parfait

C'est l'un des 7 problèmes du millénaire du Clay Institute, avec 1 million de dollars à la clé. À ce jour, un seul a été officiellement résolu : la conjecture de Poincaré, par Perelman

2. La boîte de Pandore des maths est ouverte

Des milliers de théorèmes commencent par « si l'hypothèse de Riemann est vraie, alors… »

Des générations de mathématiciens ont construit des étages entiers sur ces fondations sans savoir si elles tenaient

Si la preuve est validée, tous ces résultats deviennent vrais d'un coup. Et la version généralisée en débloque encore plus

Et je vous vois venir sur la crypto, une preuve ne casse pas RSA. Le chiffrement repose sur la difficulté de factoriser de très grands nombres, et savoir où sont les zéros ne donne aucune méthode pour le faire donc safe pour la cryptographie

3. Comment il l'a fait

Il n'y a pas de papier. Toute la preuve est publiée en Lean, le langage qui permet à un ordinateur de vérifier chaque étape, découpée en 14 archives

Il crédite Claude de plusieurs étapes clés et dit que le modèle l'a largement dépassé vers la fin. Une version lisible par un humain est promise plus tardx je pense ce soir

Alpöge a déjà un sacré palmarès cette année, voir même délirant, c'est lui qui avait réfuté la conjecture jacobienne avec Claude en juillet

4. Pourquoi il faut rester prudent

Pour l'instant, c'est une annonce. Personne en dehors de son cercle n'a encore confirmé que le code compile, ni que le théorème final dit exactement ce que dit l'hypothèse de Riemann

La communauté va tout télécharger et vérifier. Si le Lean passe, le problème serait réglé sur le plan formel avant même qu'on comprenne la preuve, une première pour un problème de ce niveau

Et le timing est hilarant encore, note sort au lendemain de l'IPO d'Anthropic, quand il faut aider le prix à monter après une première journée difficile, Il en parle lui-même dans le texte et assure que la lecture cynique est fausse

5. Elles vont toutes tomber

En octobre, OpenAI avait déjà prouvé la « quasi-hypothèse de Riemann » : une bande entière sans zéros. Alex Kontorovich (Rutgers) disait que ça vaudrait une médaille Fields instantanée si un humain l'avait fait

Terence Tao le résume très bien : on est passé de la rareté des preuves à leur abondance, et la « monnaie » des problèmes du millénaire a été « basically hyperinflated »

Yang-Mills à moitié, Navier-Stokes annoncé mais toujours contesté, et maintenant Riemann sur la table

Je vous le disais, les grands problèmes ouverts vont tomber les uns après les autres

Three weeks after Euro Pacific Bank was placed into receivership, an independent group of experienced banking professionals—including a former OCIF commissioner—approached OCIF about buying the bank.

They wanted to replace management and the board with more experienced people, fully recapitalize the bank, and cure the deficiencies OCIF cited to justify its closure. The goal was to meet regulatory requirements, protect customers, reopen the bank, and restore their access to their deposits.

Yet OCIF Commissioner Natalia I. Zequeira Díaz refused to even consider this potential rescue.

The reason is clear. Rescuing the bank conflicted with the publicity objectives of the IRS, its J5 partners, and OCIF itself. They needed a shutdown they could portray as a victory against tax evasion and money laundering. Selling and recapitalizing the bank would have undermined their effort to make an innocent bank look guilty.

The failure to allow a sale that would have fully cured all of the official deficiencies cited to justify receivership proves that those deficiencies were just a pretext. The J5 publicity stunt required the bank to be shut down, so the OCIF commissioner needed to fabricate a reason to justify it.

So Commissioner Zequeira Díaz sacrificed the interests of customers to serve a publicity campaign. The very legislative purpose of OCIF is to protect customers. Yet because of OCIF, it's now been more than four years, and only a handful of depositors have been repaid. From what I can tell, most will never get their money back.

Yet every single depositor would have been made whole had OCIF done the right thing and approved the sale, which also would have provided me with millions of dollars as the seller. Yet because the OCIF commissioner cared more about helping the J5 frame the bank than saving its customers, she rejected the sale.

So the very government entity created to protect bank customers is the reason so many have lost their deposits. This is why no one outside of Puerto Rico should bank in Puerto Rico.

posts.name: Kris Sidial
posts.text:
There’s also some irony in how foreign the idea of carry-neutral tail hedging seems to so many investors. 

In the derivatives prop trading world, traders have run long-vol books with flat carry for years. They trade vol to cover the cost of owning convexity and use that convexity to generate absolute returns.

Think about it for a second. Say you invest with a long-only equity manager. When the S&P gains 15%, the manager makes 15%. When the S&P loses 15%, the manager loses 15%. At some point, you’re going to ask, “Why am I paying for this? I can buy the index myself.”

Now imagine a long only manager who captures that same 15% on the way up and stays roughly flat on the way down. You’d understand exactly what you were paying for and ideally would be searching for managers like this. Their stock selection made a difference when the market worked against them.

So why do we drop that standard when it comes to tail hedging? When a tail program bleeds for years, investors accept “puts cost money” as an explanation. Of course puts cost money. So why aren’t we asking what the manager did to earn back that premium while keeping the convexity we hired them for?

At Ambrus, that’s the job as we see it. Trade vol well enough to preserve capital in quiet markets, participate in smaller bursts of volatility, and still own enough convexity to make a lot of money when a true tail event hits. 

If all an investor wanted was to pay premium and wait, they could do that themselves but I think the whole point of a manager is to deliver something unique and exceptional. So ideally, I don’t think the concept should be as foreign as it is to most as it’s actually the cornerstone of what hedge fund investing was built on.

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
The Fed Goes Rogue

There has been more Fedspeak in the past two weeks than in any other two-week stretch this year. Warsh appears to have a rebellion on his hands. So much for no forward guidance.

The Fed’s Keynesians are willing to risk everything, brushing aside data and theory. Headline inflation is an oil shock, not a demand boom: 3.7% against 2.6% core, with Dallas Fed trimmed-mean PCE at 2.3%. 

October’s monthly CPI slowed from 0.6% to 0.4%. Shelter, a third of the rise, is partly the Fed’s own making. Core goods rose just 0.2%, and used cars fell 1.2%. There is no evidence of second- or third-round effects.

Services excluding energy cooled to 0.3%. Services inflation of 3.2% sits below its six-decade average of 4.7%. History is clear that rate hikes don’t fix services. After the Fed began hiking in March 2022, services inflation climbed from 5.1% to 7.6% over ten months. Under Volcker, it peaked at 18.1% eight months after the October 1979 shock. Services follow wages, rents and productivity, not the last rate move.

Meanwhile, base effects are doing the tightening for them. The real policy rate, proxied by the 2-year, is 1.93%. As the energy spike drops out, it rises to as much as 3.9% by December 2027, the tightest since 1990.

Their acolytes on Wall Street amplify the noise. This is not a disciplined policy debate. It is a political institution at war with itself.

Enough monetary policy by anecdote. Show us the data. Defend the theory. Explain the policy.

Remember how this crew acted when Biden and Yellen were in charge. They embraced MMT! 

For a case study in the damage an unelected institution can do when it goes rogue, watch today’s Federal Reserve.

The direction matters more than the destination at the moment but a few crossroads approach
On 11/8 We publish "Clear Sailing" calling for a growth scare.  Red Star.  We even called for the crazy ivan rip to 7650 Green Dotted line.  Now we are back on the growth scare path in which very short stocks and moderately long bonds is the trade.  
That path could V bottom or head to recession island.  
First fork in the road is the orange dotted line in which the private economy is strong enough to reverse the growth scare.  
If it fails the growth scare becomes a growth slowdown Purple Dotted line.  
If that fails the growth slowdown reaches another fork.  The Red line is the recessionista favorite.  Stocks go down less fast but bond yields collapse. 
At that fork the policymakers intervene eventually. when they do the light blue line is the move.  We think its closer to 6000 before intervention can kick in.  
The key takeaway is the current path positioning isnt much different until the fork in the road.

Japan after 1989 illustrates precisely that dynamic, as massive fiscal deficits and monetary easing coexisted with declining government bond yields amid prolonged economic stagnation. posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
A Generational Mistake in the Making
The Fed is preparing to make a historic, generational mistake.

The real policy rate is already 1.93%, well into restrictive territory. Now the base effects are about to tighten it further, with no help from the Fed. Next spring, the war’s energy spike drops out of the inflation numbers. 

Leave policy where it is and the real rate climbs to 2.21% by the end of 2027 even if energy prices only hold flat. If energy returns to its pre-war level, it reaches 3.29%, the highest since 2000. If the energy glut pushes prices 10% below pre-war, inflation falls under 1% and the real rate hits 3.88%, the highest since 1990.
That’s the tightening coming from doing nothing. The Fed wants to hike on top of it.

Core goods inflation is 0.7%. Input prices in the New York Fed’s own survey have plunged. Oil and diesel are falling. Yet the case for hiking rests on anecdotes about AI and a fear of growth, with no evidence offered.

Arthur Burns let inflation run in the 1970s. This Fed is making the opposite mistake: hiking into falling inflation and sending real rates to levels not seen in a generation. History will not be kind.

posts.name: EndGame Macro
posts.text:
COVID Created A False Sense Of Housing Wealth And Reality Is Beginning To Set In

American homeowners are sitting on approximately $35 trillion in housing equity, equivalent to roughly 106% of U.S. GDP, near historical highs. Yet home sales relative to the number of homeowners have fallen to approximately 4.3%, near their lowest levels in decades. This extraordinary divergence reveals a housing market where enormous amounts of wealth exist on paper, but relatively few buyers are willing or financially capable of purchasing properties at current valuations.

How COVID Distorted Housing Values

The pandemic created an extraordinary environment for housing. Mortgage rates collapsed to 2.65%, fiscal stimulus expanded household purchasing power, remote work reshaped demand, and historically limited inventory intensified competition. National home prices surged approximately 42% between early 2020 and mid 2022.

Those who sold during that period converted historically elevated valuations into actual cash. But millions of homeowners who watched neighboring properties sell for extraordinary prices began treating those transactions as permanent benchmarks for their own wealth.

The problem is that the economic conditions supporting those valuations no longer exist.

Mortgage rates have climbed above 7%, dramatically reducing purchasing power. A $500,000 mortgage that cost approximately $2,015 monthly at 2.65% now costs around $3,424 at 7.28%, nearly 70% more for the exact same loan.

Yet many sellers continue expecting prices established when financing was substantially cheaper.

Why the Market Hasn’t Corrected More Aggressively

The primary reason is mortgage lock in. Millions of homeowners secured mortgages near 3%, giving them little financial incentive to sell and replace those loans at today’s rates.

This has simultaneously restricted housing supply and crushed transaction volumes, allowing elevated valuations to persist despite deteriorating affordability.

But there’s an important distinction between what homeowners believe their properties are worth and what buyers can actually afford to pay.

A home is ultimately worth what a qualified buyer is willing and able to pay, not what a neighbor received during an unprecedented period of monetary stimulus and historically cheap financing.

The Coming Repricing

Historically elevated valuations relative to household purchasing power cannot remain disconnected indefinitely. Some normalization can occur through rising wages, economic growth, and lower borrowing costs, but meaningful price corrections become increasingly plausible when demand weakens and sellers lose their ability to wait.

This is where unemployment becomes critical.

As job losses increase, households experience financial pressure, relocations become necessary, estates are liquidated, and more homeowners may be forced to accept prevailing market prices rather than wait for their preferred valuations.

Meanwhile, prospective buyers facing employment uncertainty may become even more reluctant to make the largest financial commitment of their lives, regardless of whether mortgage rates decline.

That combination could finally break the standoff between buyers and sellers.

The equity to GDP ratio does not have to mechanically return to its historical average through falling prices alone. But the underlying affordability imbalance eventually requires adjustment.

And that adjustment will not necessarily be uniform. Communities with declining populations, weaker employment prospects, and increasing housing supply could experience substantial depreciation, while desirable areas with limited inventory remain comparatively resilient.

The greatest misconception homeowners may be carrying forward from COVID is that extraordinary pandemic valuations represent a permanent measure of their wealth. Those who sold realized those prices. Those who haven’t may eventually discover that the market they remember no longer exists.

posts.name: EndGame Macro
posts.text:
At 95.7% refineries are operating near their limits, not demonstrating that supply constraints have disappeared. The EIA explicitly attributes elevated utilization to global refined product shortages and exceptionally strong diesel margins resulting from disrupted refining capacity in Russia and the Middle East. U.S. refining capacity is actually 4% below 2019 levels, while distillate inventories remain 7% below their 5 year seasonal average.

More revealing, refinery crude inputs actually declined by 129,000 barrels per day last week despite higher utilization. So how exactly does this establish that increasing production is driving prices lower rather than weakening demand coinciding with constrained refining capacity? Running refineries near maximum capacity to compensate for global supply shortages is not evidence that those shortages have been resolved. It’s evidence of how hard the remaining infrastructure is working to meet demand.
